None of them involved being fifty thousand feet up in a metal coffin, though, so that is one thing I can be somewhat grateful for.

Question of the Day #251: Do you care about seeing/hearing spoilers before watching/reading/playing something?

It’s hard to generalize about spoilers. I almost never go see new movies live in the theater (the last time I remember thinking about doing so was in 2019, but I’m unsure whether I actually did it). It’s rare for me to see a film without knowing something about it, so a lot of minor surprises have been spoiled without my caring. For a semi-recent example that’s still old enough that most people probably don’t care, when the trailers for “Spider-Man: Far from Home” came out and revealed a seeming superhero named Mysterio, anyone who knew the comics was going to have a suspicion that this character was probably not what he claimed to be. Knowing this when I finally saw the film earlier this year, I was still able to be blown away by the twist when it actually came, simply because of how good the presentation was; I knew there was a surprise, but what the surprise was exactly was still exciting to discover. But conversely, the well-known movie “The Sixth Sense” is famous for having had a once-mind-blowing twist ending, and now that pretty much everyone knows about that, I’ve never had any strong impulse to go watch it, since the twist was pretty much the whole point of that film. So really, it depends on the exact work, the narrative purpose of the twist, and the expectations surrounding it at the time.

posts.name: Jonas Ståleker
posts.cooked: Yes, I hate spoilers and I am pretty harsh when categorizing things as such. I dont want to know that a movie will surprise me in the end or that the thing we just saw will be important later. My best experiences in gaming, books, and movies have been spoiler free.

My Reply to QotD #251: I don’t actively pursue spoilers, of course. I’m not super diligent about avoiding them either, though.

Question of the Day #252: What is the optimal number of players to have in an RPG party?

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
Personally, I find it is somewhere between 1 and 5.

Seriously, not trying to be flippant! There are different benefits to different numbers, in my experience. The focused experience of smaller groups (1-3) is wonderful, while the ability to play off of others in medium-sized groups (3-5) is also great, just in a different way!

I won’t play with more than 5 if I can avoid it, though. Just too many people for me to manage and facilitate as a GM, myself.

In my experience, people drop out all the time, so it’s better to have a large number so that you can deal with no-shows. 5 or 6 is probably good; 6 means harder XP math, if you’re doing that, but otherwise it’s better to have the extra person. If your game only ever has 3 players and 2 of them don’t show up one day, you basically have no game, or a very threadbare one.

My Reply to QotD #252: I agree with @Rabit. If there are few players, then the adventure can generally be more personalized to them. But, like @The_Justifier said, it’s always good to have a buffer if there are no-shows.

Question of the Day #256: Do you read the newspaper?

Relatedly, do you think print is dead?

One day, our rich Western society will no longer be able to sustain its constant growth, and will begin to collapse. Electricity will no longer be cheap and plentiful, and access to the Internet will be a rarity at best. At that time, books will become valuable again.

So my answer to the question of “is print dead” is “that is not dead which can eternal lie*, and with strange aeons, even death may die.”

Newspapers were however always a step or three below books in terms of utility; they’re designed for cheap mass production, not permanence, and so largely replacing them with internet articles makes a bit more sense. We should probably do like a monthly or even weekly publication of information from NetNews articles in book form, for the sake of the historical record, but multiple daily papers all competing for the eyeballs of the public was never an idea that made all that much sense. Until and unless the technological collapse happens, newspapers are not particularly needed.

I read the funny pages about once a week, and an occasional variety article, but in terms of actual happenings, I wouldn’t trust the media to tell me that water is wet, so I don’t have much interest even apart from all my philosophies above.

Footnote - (brary)

Yeah, it seems kinda dumb to store so much vital information on digital systems that could easily become inaccessible.

My Reply to QotD #256: No.

Question of the Day #257: What was the best/worst prank you’ve been victim to or played on someone else?

posts.name: Rabit
posts.cooked:
One of the players in a college D&D campaign pulled an April Fool’s joke on the gaming group (which isn’t actually pertinent to this story ), so the rest of the players and I got together and started working on the next year’s event to pull on him. The player’s character was a dwarven warrior named Hendel Rockbiter who wore plate, weilded a magical hammer in one hand and a magical sword in the other, and like to open combat with “Choose your destroyer” while indicating his weapons as the choices.

I maintained notes on all the creatures and NPCs the group had previously dealt with and dealt with over the next year of play, and came up with a weird situation in which this local leader who had screwed over the PCs on their very first adventure (but promptly disappeared never to be seen again) had stolen something from Hendel and was fleeing from the PCs. Hendel had made it a practice of looking for this person everywhere they went, leaving (very bad) drawings of him on home-made “wanted” posters, so I knew it would be a good motivator.

There were three stages to the pursuit, where they would be fighting their entire way through these situations, chasing the thief the entire way:

  1. All the adversaries (except the thief) were generic, like “orcs” or “necromancers”
  2. The adversaries included minor NPCs they had encountered and defeated – but not killed – over the campaign
  3. The adversaries were the powerful villains and other NPCs they had fought and beat – in some cases, killed! – and everyone was trying to destroy the world.

For the day of the game, I made sure the other players knew what we were doing, that this was a “special” game. They played their characters in exaggerated ways, in the ways that Hendel would expect, but dialed up to 11. For example, since Hendel thought the human ranger was clumsy and kinda ridiculous, the player actually played him even more so, lying about rolls so he always failed spectacularly and making spectacularly bad decisions.

I ran the game focusing primarily on Hendel’s player, keeping him focused and attentive on the pursuit of the thief. He was building this theory that the thief had allied with their enemies to take them all down. Over the course of the pursuit, the other PCs were taken out slowly, one-by-one, but Hendel was completely driven to catch the thief, leading him into a massive combat against powerful forces of the gods all bent on global destruction, including his own god, Moradin. He defeated opponent after opponent as the world literally fell apart around him, leaving bodies and debris floating in the vast nothingness of reality.

Finally, I told him after he struck down a powerful foe (I think it was an avatar of Lolth?), that, as he looked around the remains of the battlefield, he realized there were only two entities left alive in the nothingness: Hendel and Moradin. Hendel cheered and made some comments to Moradin about how awesome he was and that they could reforge the world as it should be…

But Moradin turned towards him, a massive hammer in one hand and a powerful, glowing sword in the other, gestured with the weapons, and said “Choose your destroyer.”

Hendel’s move.

The player stared at me in complete awe, still unaware of what was going on and completely in the moment, and the combat started. For a warrior who worships combat, after all, what could be better than fighting your own god?

After a few minutes of this combat (because I realized it was almost midnight!!!), I told him he took a hit of the hammer to his head and, as everything went black, heard…

All of us yelling “April Fool’s Day!!!”

He was completely speechless. Truly.

Once he recovered (and we all stopped laughing over the ridiculousness of everything that had happened and recounting all the fun), I described how Hendel woke up with a horrible headache after a long night of eating, drinking, and brawling that had apparently caused the dream…

Or did it? There was a woman walking away, mumbling in frustration… Before vanishing as though she had never been there. (And yes, I did end up using this as part of a campaign arc. )

That was more than 30 years ago. Hendel’s player still loves talking about that session, describing it as the best TTRPG experience he’s ever had. It even came up a few weeks ago, the last time I talked to him.

That is streets ahead, @Rabit.
